definition: For popular psychology, the belief–desire–intention (BDI) model of human practical reasoning was developed by Michael Bratman as a way of explaining future-directed intention.
details: BDI is fundamentally reliant on folk psychology (the 'theory theory'), which is the notion that our mental models of the world are theories. It was used as a basis for developing the belief–desire–intention software model.

explainer.lead: The belief–desire–intention (BDI) model explains practical reasoning through three ideas: what someone believes about the world, what they want, and what they intend to do. It helps clarify how future-directed plans differ from mere wishes, and it later became the basis for a software model with the same name.

tiers.eli5: Imagine you want a snack, believe the cupboard is empty, and plan to walk to the shop. BDI separates what you think is true, what you want, and what you intend to do next. It helps explain why a want is not yet a plan.
tiers.practitioner: In BDI-style software, an engineer represents an agent's beliefs about its situation, its desired outcomes, and the future-directed intentions guiding its reasoning. A common pitfall is treating beliefs as verified facts or intentions as interchangeable with desires. The approach also inherits the assumptions of the folk-psychology view on which it is based.
tiers.paperLevel: In plain-text terms, B = beliefs about the world, D = desired outcomes, and I = future-directed intentions, with practical reasoning connecting these attitudes. Michael Bratman developed the model to explain future-directed intention. It relies on folk psychology, specifically the 'theory theory' view that our mental models of the world are theories, rather than supplying a complete formal decision rule.

explainer.example: A delivery agent believes its usual road is closed and wants to deliver a parcel on time. It forms the future-directed intention to take another route: the belief describes the situation, the desire specifies the wanted outcome, and the intention concerns what it will do.

usedIn.name: Agent software
usedIn.detail: BDI provided the basis for the belief–desire–intention software model.

usedIn.name: Practical-reasoning research
usedIn.detail: The model is used to frame explanations of future-directed human intention.

explainer.intuition: Wanting something is not the same as intending to bring it about. BDI explains practical reasoning by distinguishing an agent's view of the world and its desires from the future-directed intentions it forms.
howItWorks: Represent beliefs about how the world is.
Identify desires for how things could be.
Reason about those beliefs and desires.
explainer.whyItMatters: BDI offers a compact way to separate knowledge, motivation, and future-directed intention in accounts of practical reasoning. That distinction also made it a foundation for BDI software.
misconceptions: A desire is not already an intention.
Beliefs are an agent's mental model, not guaranteed truths.
Bratman's account of human reasoning is related to, but not identical with, the later software model.
